lesson.title: The Flattest Rule in Calculus: Why Constants Vanish
lesson.summary: The constant rule states that the derivative of any constant function is zero, because a graph that never rises or falls has zero slope everywhere.
lesson.body:
Some rules in calculus require careful algebra to uncover, but the constant rule is almost visible before you compute anything. If f(x) = c for some fixed number c, no matter what x is, the output never changes. The graph of y = c is a perfectly horizontal line, and a horizontal line has slope 0 at every single point. Since the derivative measures exactly the slope of the tangent line, it should come as no surprise that the derivative of a constant function is 0 everywhere.

The limit definition confirms this immediately, without any algebraic tricks. Let f(x) = c. Then f(x+h) is also just c, because f outputs c no matter what input it receives. The difference quotient becomes [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h = (c - c) / h = 0 / h = 0, for every nonzero h. Since this quotient equals exactly 0 before any limit is even taken, the limit as h approaches 0 of 0 is trivially 0. So f'(x) = 0 for all x. There is no approximation happening here: the difference quotient is not merely close to 0, it literally equals 0 at every step, which is what makes this the simplest of all the derivative rules to prove.

As a concrete example, let f(x) = 7. This function outputs 7 regardless of whether x is -100, 0, or a million. Its graph is the horizontal line y = 7, and its derivative is f'(x) = 0 for every x. You can check this against the limit definition directly: f(x+h) - f(x) = 7 - 7 = 0, divided by h gives 0, and the limit of 0 is 0. There is nothing further to simplify.

This rule connects directly back to the derivative rules chapter's worked example, f(x) = 3x^2 + 2. When that computation was carried out from the limit definition, the constant term 2 disappeared in the very first subtraction step, f(x+h) - f(x), because 2 subtracted from 2 leaves 0 regardless of h. That cancellation was not a coincidence specific to the number 2: it is the constant rule playing out inside a larger computation. Any constant added anywhere in a function contributes exactly 0 to the derivative, which is why constants can simply be dropped once you start differentiating term by term.

It is worth being precise about what "constant" means here: a fixed real number that does not depend on x, such as 7, -3, or pi. It does not include expressions that merely look simple but still involve x, such as 0 times x or x divided by x for x not equal to 0, since those still describe functions whose value could in principle depend on the input even if it happens not to. Once a term is confirmed to be a genuine constant, its derivative contribution is always 0, and that fact will be used constantly, so to speak, once the sum, difference, and constant multiple rules let you break complicated functions into simpler pieces.

A second short example makes the pattern even clearer. Let f(x) = -3, a negative constant. Following the same steps, f(x+h) - f(x) = -3 - (-3) = 0, and 0 divided by h is still 0 for every nonzero h, so f'(x) = 0. The sign of the constant never enters the computation at all, since the two copies of c cancel completely before any limit is taken. This is different from most other derivative rules, where the specific value of a number, such as an exponent or a coefficient, changes the resulting formula. Here the value of c is completely irrelevant to the outcome, which is part of what makes the constant rule the most immediate and least fragile rule in the entire toolkit of differentiation.
